title: Power analysis by simulation
text:
Power formulas exist for simple designs such as t-tests. For the models most CBB projects need (repeated observations of the same animals, counts, binary choices), they do not. Simulation works for every model: simulate data from the planned model many times, fit the model to each dataset, and count how often the effect is detected.
This follows directly from the guiding principle model before data, and the simulation code doubles as a first draft of the analysis script and of the preregistration.

title: Power analysis by simulation
text:
Simulate first
How does power change with the number of animals, when each animal is tested in 10 trials?

library(lme4)
set.seed(14)

power_lmm <- function(n_id, n_trials = 10, b1 = 0.6, sd_id = 0.6, nsim = 200) {
  mean(replicate(nsim, {
    id <- factor(rep(1:n_id, each = n_trials))
    x  <- rep(rep(0:1, length.out = n_id), each = n_trials) # between-animal condition
    u  <- rep(rnorm(n_id, 0, sd_id), each = n_trials)
    y  <- b1 * x + u + rnorm(n_id * n_trials)
    m1 <- lmer(y ~ x + (1 | id), REML = FALSE)
    m0 <- lmer(y ~ 1 + (1 | id), REML = FALSE)
    anova(m0, m1)$`Pr(>Chisq)`[2] < .05
  }))
}

n_ids <- c(10, 20, 30, 40, 60, 80)
pow   <- sapply(n_ids, power_lmm)

plot(n_ids, pow, type = "b", pch = 19, col = "#1b6f8a", ylim = c(0, 1),
     xlab = "Number of animals", ylab = "Power")
abline(h = .8, lty = 2, col = "#c0392b")

title: Bayesian modelling with brms
text:
brms is an R package for fitting Bayesian regression models, from simple linear models to complex multilevel models. You write the same formula syntax as in lme4, e.g. y ~ x + (1 | id). brms translates the model into Stan, which estimates the posterior distribution of all parameters.
This makes brms an easy entry into Bayesian modelling for anyone who knows the models from Linear Models in R: the models stay the same, only the way of estimating them and of drawing conclusions changes.

section: Worked example: the Safe-vs-Risky box study
text:
Worked example: the Safe-vs-Risky box study
We return to the example from session 11, with the same data. Chimpanzees choose into which of two boxes a grape is dropped. The Safe box clearly guarantees delivery; in the Risky box, the grape seems to get stuck. In fact, both boxes always deliver.


RQ1: Do chimps prefer the Safe box in session 1?

RQ2: Does this preference change over sessions?


The study (with the MPI EVA, Leipzig) is preregistered, but the data do not exist yet. As in session 11, the numbers are made up to reflect what we expect: 10 chimps × 4 sessions × 10 trials; response: choice (1 = Safe, 0 = Risky).

The data

Data (same as session 11)# Safe choices (out of 10) of 10 chimps in sessions 1-4
K <- rbind(c( 9, 10, 10, 10), c(10,  9,  9,  8), c(10, 10,  9,  7), c(10, 10,  6,  8),
           c( 5,  8,  8,  8), c( 8,  6,  6,  3), c( 5,  3,  2,  4), c( 5,  2,  3,  3),
           c( 1,  0,  1,  0), c( 1,  0,  0,  0))
cd <- data.frame(chimp = factor(rep(1:10, 4)), session = rep(1:4, each = 10), safe = c(K))

# trial-level data: one row per choice
set.seed(11)
trials <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(cd)), function(i)
  data.frame(chimp = cd$chimp[i], session = cd$session[i],
             trial = (cd$session[i] - 1) * 10 + 1:10,
             choice = sample(rep(c(1, 0), c(cd$safe[i], 10 - cd$safe[i]))))))
trials$session_c <- trials$session - 1          # session 1 = 0



Codecd$p <- cd$safe / 10
avg  <- aggregate(p ~ session, data = cd, FUN = mean)

ggplot(cd, aes(session, p)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = .5, linetype = 2, colour = col_muted) +
  geom_line(aes(group = chimp), colour = col_teal, alpha = .35) +
  geom_line(data = avg, colour = col_red, linewidth = 1.3) +
  geom_point(data = avg, colour = col_red, size = 2.5) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Session", y = "Safe choices",
       subtitle = "Thin lines: individual chimps · red: average")







Step 1: the GLMM from session 11

glmm <- glmer(choice ~ session_c + (1 + session_c | chimp),
              family = binomial, data = trials,
              control = glmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa"))

Step 2: priors
A Bayesian model needs a prior for every parameter. We use weakly informative priors on the log-odds scale: they rule out absurd values but leave the data in charge.

priors <- c(prior(normal(0, 1.5), class = "Intercept"),   # P(Safe) in session 1
            prior(normal(0, 1),   class = "b"),           # change per session
            prior(exponential(0.5), class = "sd"),        # between-chimp SDs (mean 2)
            prior(lkj(2),         class = "cor"))         # intercept-slope correlation

What do these priors imply before seeing any data? A prior predictive check translates them into chimp-level choice probabilities in session 1:

Codeset.seed(1)
p_session1 <- plogis(rnorm(1e4, 0, 1.5) + rnorm(1e4, 0, rexp(1e4, 0.5)))
ggplot(data.frame(p = p_session1), aes(p)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = col_teal, colour = "white") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = "P(Safe) in session 1 for a chimp, implied by the priors", y = NULL) +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank())







The priors allow chimps with strong Safe or strong Risky preferences, as in our data, where some chimps almost always and others almost never choose Safe.
Step 3: fit the model
The formula is exactly the one from glmer(). bernoulli is the binomial family for single 0/1 choices.

fit <- brm(choice ~ session_c + (1 + session_c | chimp),
           family = bernoulli, data = trials, prior = priors,
           chains = 4, iter = 2000, cores = 4, seed = 2026)


summary(fit)

#>  Family: bernoulli 
#>   Links: mu = logit 
#> Formula: choice ~ session_c + (1 + session_c | chimp) 
#>    Data: trials (Number of observations: 400) 
#>   Draws: 4 chains, each with iter = 2000; warmup = 1000; thin = 1;
#>          total post-warmup draws = 4000
#> 
#> Group-Level Effects: 
#> ~chimp (Number of levels: 10) 
#>                          Estimate Est.Error l-95% CI u-95% CI Rhat Bulk_ESS
#> sd(Intercept)                2.58      0.71     1.54     4.41 1.00     1753
#> sd(session_c)                0.45      0.30     0.03     1.16 1.00     1008
#> cor(Intercept,session_c)    -0.01      0.40    -0.75     0.71 1.00     3411
#>                          Tail_ESS
#> sd(Intercept)                2042
#> sd(session_c)                1323
#> cor(Intercept,session_c)     2310
#> 
#> Population-Level Effects: 
#>           Estimate Est.Error l-95% CI u-95% CI Rhat Bulk_ESS Tail_ESS
#> Intercept     0.79      0.78    -0.77     2.42 1.01     1025     1427
#> session_c    -0.37      0.22    -0.83     0.02 1.00     1947     1639
#> 
#> Draws were sampled using sampling(NUTS). For each parameter, Bulk_ESS
#> and Tail_ESS are effective sample size measures, and Rhat is the potential
#> scale reduction factor on split chains (at convergence, Rhat = 1).


All Rhat values are close to 1.00 and the effective sample sizes (ESS) are large, so the four chains agree. The trace plots should look like “hairy caterpillars”, with no chain drifting off:

Codebayesplot::mcmc_trace(as.array(fit), pars = c("b_Intercept", "b_session_c", "sd_chimp__session_c"),
                      facet_args = list(ncol = 3)) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")







Step 4: answer the research questions with the posterior
The posterior is a distribution, so we can answer the research questions on the response scale and as probabilities.

draws <- as_draws_df(fit)
p1 <- plogis(draws$b_Intercept)                            # session 1, average chimp
p4 <- plogis(draws$b_Intercept + 3 * draws$b_session_c)    # session 4, average chimp


Codepost <- rbind(data.frame(session = "Session 1", p = p1), data.frame(session = "Session 4", p = p4))
ggplot(post, aes(p, fill = session)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = .5, linetype = 2, colour = col_muted) +
  geom_density(alpha = .6, colour = NA) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(col_teal, col_red), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "P(Safe) for an average chimp", y = "Posterior density")









RQ1: In session 1, an average chimp chooses the Safe box with probability 0.68, 95% credible interval [0.32, 0.92]. The posterior probability that the average chimp prefers Safe, i.e. that P(Safe) > .5, is 0.86. The interval is wide: with chimps that differ this much, 10 chimps say little about the average chimp’s preference.

RQ2: The change per session is -0.36 on the log-odds scale, 95% CrI [-0.83, 0.02]; the posterior probability of a decline is 0.97. From session 1 to session 4, P(Safe) changes by -0.23 for the average chimp, 95% CrI [-0.51, 0.01].

The model-implied curve for the average chimp, with 95% credible band:

Codece <- conditional_effects(fit, effects = "session_c")$session_c
ggplot(ce, aes(session_c + 1, estimate__)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = .5, linetype = 2, colour = col_muted) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lower__, ymax = upper__), fill = col_teal, alpha = .25) +
  geom_line(colour = col_teal, linewidth = 1.2) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Session", y = "P(Safe)")







Step 5: does the model reproduce the data?
A posterior predictive check simulates new datasets from the fitted model and compares them with the observed data. Here: the proportion of Safe choices for each chimp.

Codepp_check(fit, type = "stat_grouped", stat = "mean", group = "chimp", ndraws = 1000) +
  facet_wrap(~ group, ncol = 5) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, .5, 1), labels = c("0", ".5", "1")) +
  labs(x = "Proportion of Safe choices") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")







The observed proportions (dark lines) lie well within the simulated ones for every chimp.
Step 6: comparison with the GLMM from session 11

Codefe_b <- fixef(fit)
vc   <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(glmm))
sd_b <- summary(fit)$random$chimp

tab <- data.frame(
  Parameter = c("Intercept (session 1)", "Session", "SD intercept", "SD session slope", "Correlation"),
  glmer     = c(paste0(f2(cf[, 1]), " [", f2(ci[, 1]), ", ", f2(ci[, 2]), "]"),
                f2(vc$sdcor[1]), f2(vc$sdcor[2]), f2(vc$sdcor[3])),

                     f2(c(fe_b[, 3], sd_b[, 3])), ", ", f2(c(fe_b[, 4], sd_b[, 4])), "]"))

  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = col_muted) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi), position = position_dodge(width = .5)) +

  labs(x = "Estimate (log-odds) with 95% interval", y = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")







What stays the same, and what changes


The estimates agree, the intervals differ. The posterior means are close to the glmer() estimates: Bayesian modelling is not a different model, but a different way of estimating it. The credible interval for the session effect is wider and just includes zero. The Wald interval of glmer() treats the estimated between-chimp SDs as known; the posterior also carries their uncertainty, which is large with only 10 chimps.

The interpretation changes. A 95% credible interval contains the parameter with 95% probability, given model and priors. That is how most people (mis)read a confidence interval anyway. And we can directly state things like “the probability that the preference declines over sessions is 0.97”.

Uncertainty about the variance components is visible. glmer() gives only point estimates for the between-chimp SDs and their correlation; brms gives full intervals. The wide intervals show how little 10 chimps tell us about individual differences.

Complex random-effects structures become easier. With only 10 individuals, glmer() often runs into convergence warnings or singular fits. The priors keep brms stable, which helps with the maximal random-effects structures recommended for confirmatory tests.

The price: more computing time (here a few minutes instead of a second) and the need to choose and justify priors.

title: Testing for Absence and Equivalence
text: A hands-on course that builds on Linear Models in R. Many hypotheses in behavioural research predict the absence of an effect, yet a non-significant result is often misread as evidence for it. The course teaches two ways to test such predictions properly: frequentist equivalence tests and Bayesian alternatives.

title: Testing for Absence and Equivalence
text:
Topics

Why p > .05 is not evidence for “no effect”: absence of evidence vs. evidence of absence.
The smallest effect size of interest (SESOI): how to justify which effects are too small to matter.
Equivalence tests (TOST): how to test predictions of “no effect” with classical significance tests, based on a justified SESOI (R package TOSTER).
Bayes factors: quantifying the evidence for the null relative to the alternative (R package BayesFactor).
Bayesian estimation with a region of practical equivalence (ROPE): deciding on the basis of the posterior distribution (R packages brms and bayestestR).
Comparing the approaches: when they agree, when they differ, and the role of priors.

Outcome: each participant plans how to test a “no effect” prediction in their own project, including a sample-size justification.

Key terms: p-value, SESOI (smallest effect size of interest), Equivalence test (TOST), Bayes factor, ROPE (region of practical equivalence), Prior, posterior

title: Testing for Absence and Equivalence
text:
Four tests, one dataset
Classical significance tests can do much more than reject an effect of exactly zero. Lakens (2022, ch. 9) distinguishes four kinds of tests. They differ only in which hypothesis is tested, so all four can be applied to the same data: each answers a different question.

The data
Participants solve a puzzle; we measure the solution time in seconds. A control group is compared with a training group (500 participants each). The effect of interest is the time saved by training, Δ = control − training.

The smallest effect size of interest (SESOI) is 2 seconds: savings below 2 s are too small to matter in practice.
A theory predicts savings between 0.5 and 2.5 s.


set.seed(4)
control  <- rnorm(500, mean = 20,   sd = 5)
training <- rnorm(500, mean = 18.8, sd = 5)

sesoi <- 2                     # smallest effect size of interest (s)
lower <- 0.5; upper <- 2.5     # range predicted by the theory (s)

The observed saving is Δ = 1.25 s, 95% CI [0.65, 1.85], 90% CI [0.75, 1.76].


The four tests at a glance


Code
lim <- c(-4, 4)
panels <- c("A: two-sided null hypothesis test", "B: interval hypothesis test",
            "C: equivalence test", "D: minimum effect test")
reg <- function(panel, xmin, xmax, hyp) data.frame(panel, xmin, xmax, hyp)
regions <- rbind(
  reg(panels[1], lim[1], lim[2], "H1"),
  reg(panels[2], c(lim[1], upper), c(lower, lim[2]), "H0"), reg(panels[2], lower, upper, "H1"),
  reg(panels[3], c(lim[1], sesoi), c(-sesoi, lim[2]), "H1"), reg(panels[3], -sesoi, sesoi, "H0"),
  reg(panels[4], c(lim[1], sesoi), c(-sesoi, lim[2]), "H1"), reg(panels[4], -sesoi, sesoi, "H0"))
regions$hyp[regions$panel == panels[3]] <- ifelse(regions$hyp[regions$panel == panels[3]] == "H0", "H1", "H0")
regions$panel <- factor(regions$panel, levels = panels)
nil <- data.frame(panel = factor(panels[1], levels = panels), x = 0)
ci  <- data.frame(panel = factor(panels, levels = panels), est = est,
                  lo = c(t95$conf.int[1], rep(t90$conf.int[1], 3)),
                  hi = c(t95$conf.int[2], rep(t90$conf.int[2], 3)))

ggplot() +
  geom_rect(data = regions, aes(xmin = xmin, xmax = xmax, ymin = -.4, ymax = .4, fill = hyp), alpha = .35) +
  geom_segment(data = nil, aes(x = x, xend = x, y = -.4, yend = .4), colour = col_h0, linewidth = 1.6) +
  geom_errorbarh(data = ci, aes(y = 0, xmin = lo, xmax = hi), height = .25, linewidth = 1, colour = col_navy) +
  geom_point(data = ci, aes(est, 0), size = 2.6, colour = col_navy) +
  facet_wrap(~ panel, ncol = 1, strip.position = "left", dir = "v") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(H0 = col_h0, H1 = col_h1), name = NULL,
                    labels = c(H0 = "null hypothesis (H0)", H1 = "alternative hypothesis (H1)")) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(-sesoi, 0, lower, sesoi, upper), labels = c("-2", "0", "0.5", "2", "2.5"),
                     limits = lim, expand = c(0, 0)) +
  labs(x = expression(paste("Time saved by training, ", Delta, " (s)")), y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(), panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(), panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        strip.text.y.left = element_text(angle = 0, hjust = 1, face = "bold"),
        legend.position = "top")








Figure 1: Two-sided null hypothesis test (A), interval hypothesis test (B), equivalence test (C) and minimum effect test (D). Red: values in the null hypothesis; blue: values in the alternative hypothesis. Point and bar: our estimate with 95% CI (A) or 90% CI (B–D). Adapted from Lakens (2022), Fig. 9.1; this figure is licensed CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.







A: two-sided null hypothesis test
Question: Is there any effect at all? H0: Δ = 0. H1: Δ ≠ 0. The classic t-test; significant if the 95% CI excludes 0.

t.test(control, training, var.equal = TRUE)

#> 
#>  Two Sample t-test
#> 
#> data:  control and training
#> t = 4.0852, df = 998, p-value = 4.757e-05
#> alternative hypothesis: true difference in means is not equal to 0
#> 95 percent confidence interval:
#>  0.6510149 1.8545975
#> sample estimates:
#> mean of x mean of y 
#>  19.85426  18.60146


Result: p < .001. Training saves time, but this test says nothing about whether the saving is large enough to matter.


B: interval hypothesis test
Question: Does the effect fall within the range the theory predicts? H0: Δ ≤ 0.5 or Δ ≥ 2.5. H1: 0.5 < Δ < 2.5. Two one-sided tests, one against each bound; the prediction is supported if both are significant, i.e. the 90% CI lies inside the predicted range.

# H0a: Delta <= 0.5 (test: greater than the lower bound)
p_lo <- t.test(control, training, mu = lower,
               alternative = "greater", var.equal = TRUE)$p.value
# H0b: Delta >= 2.5 (test: less than the upper bound)
p_hi <- t.test(control, training, mu = upper,
               alternative = "less", var.equal = TRUE)$p.value
c(p_lower = p_lo, p_upper = p_hi, p = max(p_lo, p_hi))

#>      p_lower      p_upper            p 
#> 7.133457e-03 2.569832e-05 7.133457e-03


Result: p = .007. The saving lies within the predicted range of 0.5 to 2.5 s.


C: equivalence test (TOST)
Question: Is the effect too small to matter? H0: Δ ≤ −2 or Δ ≥ 2. H1: −2 < Δ < 2. The same two one-sided tests as in B, now against −SESOI and +SESOI; equivalence is shown if the 90% CI lies inside the equivalence bounds.

# H0a: Delta <= -2 (test: greater than the lower equivalence bound)
p_lo <- t.test(control, training, mu = -sesoi,
               alternative = "greater", var.equal = TRUE)$p.value
# H0b: Delta >= 2 (test: less than the upper equivalence bound)
p_hi <- t.test(control, training, mu = sesoi,
               alternative = "less", var.equal = TRUE)$p.value
c(p_lower = p_lo, p_upper = p_hi, p = max(p_lo, p_hi))

#>      p_lower      p_upper            p 
#> 2.791839e-25 7.502522e-03 7.502522e-03


Result: p = .008. The saving is statistically equivalent to zero within ±2 s: it is real (test A), but smaller than anything we consider meaningful.


D: minimum effect test
Question: Is the effect larger than the smallest effect of interest? H0: −2 ≤ Δ ≤ 2. H1: Δ < −2 or Δ > 2. The reverse of the equivalence test; here we test only the direction the theory predicts (Δ > 2).

# H0: Delta <= 2 (test: greater than the SESOI)
t.test(control, training, mu = sesoi,
       alternative = "greater", var.equal = TRUE)$p.value

#> [1] 0.9924975


Result: p = .992. We cannot claim a saving larger than 2 s.


With the TOSTER package
The R package TOSTER runs tests C and D in one call and adds effect sizes and plots:

library(TOSTER)
# C: equivalence test
t_TOST(x = control, y = training, eqb = sesoi, var.equal = TRUE)
# D: minimum effect test
t_TOST(x = control, y = training, eqb = sesoi, var.equal = TRUE, hypothesis = "MET")

rejected: prediction supported


C: equivalence test
Too small to matter?
|Δ| ≥ 2
rejected: equivalent to zero


D: minimum effect test
Larger than the SESOI?
|Δ| ≤ 2
not rejected



The same data give four different answers because the tests ask four different questions. Which test is appropriate follows from the hypothesis, and should be decided, and preregistered, before the data are seen.

Note: With 500 participants per group, even a saving of about 1 s is detected (A) and shown to be negligible (C). With small samples, typical for animal studies, all four tests are often inconclusive. Planning the sample size for the test you intend to run is part of the course.

Reference: Lakens, D. (2022). Improving your statistical inferences (ch. 9: Equivalence testing and interval hypotheses). https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.6409077. Licensed CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.

title: Testing for Absence and Equivalence
section: Simulate first: three answers to the same data
text:
Simulate first: three answers to the same data
There is no difference between the two groups in these data. The classic t-test is non-significant, but that alone says nothing about whether the effect is absent.

set.seed(13)
n <- 100
a <- rnorm(n); b <- rnorm(n)                 # true difference = 0
sesoi <- 0.4                                 # smallest effect of interest (in SD units)

# 1. Classic t-test: non-significant, but not evidence for "no effect"
t.test(a, b, var.equal = TRUE)$p.value

#> [1] 0.5200304

# 2. Equivalence test (TOST): is the difference within [-SESOI, +SESOI]?
p_lower <- t.test(a, b, mu = -sesoi, alternative = "greater", var.equal = TRUE)$p.value
p_upper <- t.test(a, b, mu =  sesoi, alternative = "less",    var.equal = TRUE)$p.value
max(p_lower, p_upper)                        # < .05 -> effect is statistically equivalent to zero

#> [1] 0.01766867

# 3. Bayes factor for H0 over H1 (BIC approximation; Wagenmakers, 2007)
d  <- data.frame(y = c(a, b), group = rep(c("a", "b"), each = n))
m0 <- lm(y ~ 1, data = d)
m1 <- lm(y ~ group, data = d)
exp((BIC(m1) - BIC(m0)) / 2)                 # BF01 > 1 favours "no difference"

#> [1] 11.46872


In the course, the BIC approximation is replaced by Bayes factors with explicit priors (BayesFactor) and by posterior estimation with a ROPE (brms, bayestestR).

title: Open, Replicable, and Ethical Science
text:
Topics


Preregistration and registered reports, including for observational field data and secondary analyses.

Sequential analyses: group-sequential designs with planned interim analyses and alpha spending, so data collection can stop early for efficacy without inflating the type I error.

Optional stopping and stopping for futility: why peeking at p-values inflates error rates (shown by simulation), and how to stop correctly, including when an effect is unlikely to emerge.


Why this matters at DPZ: sequential designs and stopping for futility reduce the expected number of animals per study. This directly supports the Reduction principle of the 3Rs and strengthens the justification in animal-ethics applications.

Outcome: each participant drafts a preregistration with a sample-size or sequential plan for their own project.

title: Open, Replicable, and Ethical Science
section: Simulate first: why peeking is a problem
text:
Simulate first: why peeking is a problem
There is no effect in these simulations. A researcher tests after every 10 observations per group and stops as soon as p < .05. How often do they find a “significant” result?

set.seed(12)
looks <- seq(10, 100, by = 10)
nsim  <- 2000

first_sig <- replicate(nsim, {
  a <- rnorm(max(looks)); b <- rnorm(max(looks))       # H0 is true
  p <- sapply(looks, function(n) t.test(a[1:n], b[1:n])$p.value)
  which(p < .05)[1]                                    # first look with p < .05 (NA if none)
})

alpha_by_look <- sapply(seq_along(looks), function(k) mean(!is.na(first_sig) & first_sig <= k))

plot(looks, alpha_by_look, type = "b", pch = 19, col = "#c0392b", ylim = c(0, .25),
     xlab = "Maximum n per group (one look every 10)", ylab = "Type I error rate")
abline(h = .05, lty = 2, col = "#1b6f8a")







With ten looks, the false-positive rate is far above the nominal 5 %. Group-sequential designs (e.g., with rpact) fix this by spending the alpha across the planned looks.

title: 10 · Generalized linear models (GLM)
section: Worked example 1: who solves the puzzle box?
text:
Worked example 1: who solves the puzzle box?
120 monkeys are each tested once with a new puzzle box. Do younger monkeys solve novel problems more often? The response is binary: solved (1) or not (0). The data are simulated.

set.seed(10)
puzzle <- data.frame(age = round(runif(120, 2, 22), 1))
puzzle$age_c  <- puzzle$age - 10                     # centred at 10 years
puzzle$solved <- rbinom(120, 1, plogis(0.4 - 0.18 * puzzle$age_c))


Logistic regression
The binomial distribution with the logit link: logit(p) = log(p / (1 − p)) = β0 + β1 · age.

glm1 <- glm(solved ~ age_c, family = binomial, data = puzzle)
summary(glm1)$coefficients

#>               Estimate Std. Error   z value     Pr(>|z|)
#> (Intercept)  0.4815479 0.21833960  2.205500 2.741906e-02
#> age_c       -0.1982492 0.04362213 -4.544693 5.501545e-06

exp(coef(glm1))        # odds ratios

#> (Intercept)       age_c 
#>   1.6185778   0.8201655



Intercept 0.48: the log-odds of solving for a 10-year-old, i.e. P(solved) = plogis(0.48) = 62%.
Slope -0.20 per year; odds ratio 0.82: with each year, the odds of solving are multiplied by 0.82. Odds are not probabilities: how much the probability changes depends on where you are on the S-curve. A rule of thumb: β/4 ≈ -0.05 is the maximum change in probability per year (at 50%).



Predictions on the response scale
Compute the confidence interval on the link scale, then back-transform, so that it stays within 0–1:

nd <- data.frame(age = seq(2, 22, by = 0.2)); nd$age_c <- nd$age - 10
pr <- predict(glm1, newdata = nd, type = "link", se.fit = TRUE)
nd$p  <- plogis(pr$fit)
nd$lo <- plogis(pr$fit - 1.96 * pr$se.fit)
nd$hi <- plogis(pr$fit + 1.96 * pr$se.fit)

ggplot(nd, aes(age, p)) +
  geom_jitter(data = puzzle, aes(age, solved), height = .03, width = 0, colour = col_lm, alpha = .5) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = col_glm, alpha = .2) +
  geom_line(colour = col_glm, linewidth = 1.2) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = "Age (years)", y = "P(solved)")










Test: likelihood-ratio test

glm0 <- glm(solved ~ 1, family = binomial, data = puzzle)
anova(glm0, glm1, test = "Chisq")

#> Analysis of Deviance Table
#> 
#> Model 1: solved ~ 1
#> Model 2: solved ~ age_c
#>   Resid. Df Resid. Dev Df Deviance  Pr(>Chi)    
#> 1       119     165.52                          
#> 2       118     139.51  1   26.012 3.393e-07 ***
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

title: 10 · Generalized linear models (GLM)
section: Worked example 2: grunts in focal observations
text:
Worked example 2: grunts in focal observations
90 monkeys are each observed once, for 10–60 minutes, and we count their grunts. Do higher-ranking monkeys grunt more? The data are simulated.

set.seed(3)
calls <- data.frame(rank_z = round(rnorm(90), 2), minutes = round(runif(90, 10, 60)))
mu    <- calls$minutes * exp(log(0.15) + 0.35 * calls$rank_z)
calls$grunts <- rnbinom(90, mu = mu, size = 2)          # overdispersed counts


Poisson regression with an offset
The Poisson distribution with the log link. Because observation times differ, offset(log(minutes)) turns the model of counts into a model of rates (grunts per minute).

pois <- glm(grunts ~ rank_z + offset(log(minutes)), family = poisson, data = calls)
summary(pois)$coefficients

#>               Estimate Std. Error    z value     Pr(>|z|)
#> (Intercept) -1.7599468 0.04414725 -39.865381 0.000000e+00
#> rank_z       0.4046258 0.04999826   8.092797 5.831013e-16

exp(coef(pois))        # rate per minute (intercept) and rate ratio (rank)

#> (Intercept)      rank_z 
#>    0.172054    1.498742


An average-ranking monkey grunts 0.17 times per minute (10.3 per hour); one SD higher rank multiplies the rate by 1.50.


Overdispersion
The Poisson model assumes that the variance equals the mean. The dispersion ratio should be close to 1:

sum(residuals(pois, type = "pearson")^2) / df.residual(pois)

#> [1] 3.968674


At 3.97, the counts vary much more than the model expects, so its standard errors are too small. Simulated quantile residuals show the same (plot(DHARMa::simulateResiduals(pois))). A negative binomial model adds a parameter for the extra variance:

nb <- glm.nb(grunts ~ rank_z + offset(log(minutes)), data = calls)
summary(nb)$coefficients

#>              Estimate Std. Error    z value     Pr(>|z|)
#> (Intercept) -1.783289  0.0916880 -19.449539 2.940641e-84
#> rank_z       0.392227  0.1059704   3.701287 2.145085e-04


The estimate for rank hardly changes (0.39 vs. 0.40), but its standard error more than doubles (0.106 vs. 0.050). Here the effect survives; with a weaker or no effect, the Poisson model could easily produce a false positive (see the simulation in the slides).

title: 10 · Generalized linear models (GLM)
section: Practical: maternal approaches in wild Guinea baboons
text:
Practical: maternal approaches in wild Guinea baboons
How often do mothers approach their infants in the first six months of life, and does this depend on the infant’s sex or on the mother’s age? You use real field data from the DPZ field station Simenti (Senegal):

Dal Pesco, F., et al. (2026). Maternal style does not predict infant growth and survival in wild Guinea baboons. Animal Behaviour.

The data are openly available on OSF (https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/YH2BW). Please cite the paper and the repository when you use them.
Download dataset_mothering_behaviors_Anonymized.csv
The file has one row per infant and month. To keep the observations independent (the topic of session 11), we first aggregate the data to one row per infant: all approaches and all observation time in the first six months. The variables you need:







Variable
Meaning




immature_ID
infant ID


mother_ID
mother ID


age
infant age in days


immature_sex
infant sex (F, M)


mother_monthly_age
mother’s age class in this month: young (YAF), middle-aged (MAF), old (OAF) adult female


imm_focal_duration_sec
focal observation time in this month (seconds)


normal_approach_received_freq
number of approaches received from the mother




xdata <- read.csv("dataset_mothering_behaviors_Anonymized.csv")


Exercise 1: one row per infant
Keep the months in which the infant was younger than six months (age < 183 days). Then aggregate to one row per infant with the total number of approaches, the total observation time in hours, the infant’s sex and the mother’s (most frequent) age class.






Solution






xdata <- xdata[, !duplicated(names(xdata))]          # 'immature_ID' appears twice
w <- xdata[xdata$age < 183, ]

infants <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(w, w$immature_ID), function(d) data.frame(
  infant     = d$immature_ID[1],
  mother     = d$mother_ID[1],
  sex        = d$immature_sex[1],
  mother_age = names(which.max(table(d$mother_monthly_age))),
  hours      = sum(d$imm_focal_duration_sec) / 3600,
  approaches = sum(d$normal_approach_received_freq))))
infants$mother_age <- factor(infants$mother_age, levels = c("MAF", "YAF", "OAF"))  # most common class as reference
infants$sex <- factor(infants$sex)

nrow(infants)

#> [1] 68

table(infants$sex, infants$mother_age)

#>    
#>     MAF YAF OAF
#>   F  21   9   6
#>   M  24   4   4







Exercise 2: explore the data
Plot the number of approaches against observation time, and the rate (approaches per hour) by sex and mother’s age class. What do you notice about the distribution of the counts?






Solution






summary(infants$approaches)

#>    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
#>   0.000   0.000   1.000   4.662   5.000  39.000

mean(infants$approaches == 0)                        # proportion of zeros

#> [1] 0.3823529

infants$rate <- infants$approaches / infants$hours
ggplot(infants, aes(mother_age, rate, colour = sex)) +
  geom_jitter(width = .15, alpha = .7, size = 2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(col_glm, col_red)) +
  labs(x = "Mother's age class", y = "Approaches per hour")








The counts are small, skewed and contain many zeros, and observation time varies a lot between infants: a count model with an offset is needed.





Exercise 3: a Poisson GLM
Fit a Poisson GLM of approaches with sex and mother_age as predictors and the appropriate offset. Interpret the coefficients as rate ratios and test both predictors with likelihood-ratio tests.






Solution






pois_b <- glm(approaches ~ sex + mother_age + offset(log(hours)),
              family = poisson, data = infants)
summary(pois_b)$coefficients

#>                  Estimate Std. Error    z value  Pr(>|z|)
#> (Intercept)    0.19998044 0.09690815  2.0636080 0.0390549
#> sexM           0.08873380 0.11676871  0.7599107 0.4473079
#> mother_ageYAF -0.08850002 0.15126632 -0.5850610 0.5585067
#> mother_ageOAF -0.50930028 0.23206578 -2.1946376 0.0281896

exp(coef(pois_b))                                     # rate ratios

#>   (Intercept)          sexM mother_ageYAF mother_ageOAF 
#>     1.2213789     1.0927897     0.9153031     0.6009159

drop1(pois_b, test = "Chisq")                         # LRT for each predictor

#> Single term deletions
#> 
#> Model:
#> approaches ~ sex + mother_age + offset(log(hours))
#>            Df Deviance    AIC    LRT Pr(>Chi)  
#> <none>          173.49 317.28                  
#> sex         1   174.07 315.86 0.5792   0.4466  
#> mother_age  2   179.00 318.79 5.5165   0.0634 .
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


Taken at face value, infants of old mothers (OAF) receive about 40% fewer approaches than infants of middle-aged mothers (MAF; Wald test p < .05), although the overall likelihood-ratio test of mother_age is only marginal. But can we trust these standard errors?





Exercise 4: check the model
Compute the dispersion ratio. If DHARMa is installed, also look at the simulated residuals.






Solution






sum(residuals(pois_b, type = "pearson")^2) / df.residual(pois_b)

#> [1] 2.554734



library(DHARMa)
plot(simulateResiduals(pois_b))
testDispersion(simulateResiduals(pois_b))

The dispersion ratio is well above 1: the data are overdispersed, and the Poisson standard errors are too small.





Exercise 5: a negative binomial GLM
Fit the same model as a negative binomial GLM. Compare the estimates, standard errors and tests with the Poisson model. Does your conclusion change?






Solution






nb_b <- glm.nb(approaches ~ sex + mother_age + offset(log(hours)), data = infants)
summary(nb_b)$coefficients

#>                  Estimate Std. Error     z value  Pr(>|z|)
#> (Intercept)    0.02966697  0.2120112  0.13993111 0.8887144
#> sexM           0.02279024  0.2620325  0.08697484 0.9306915
#> mother_ageYAF -0.03990511  0.3376029 -0.11820133 0.9059081
#> mother_ageOAF -0.40752939  0.3941762 -1.03387623 0.3011940

nb_b$theta

#> [1] 1.765522

drop1(nb_b, test = "Chisq")

#> Single term deletions
#> 
#> Model:
#> approaches ~ sex + mother_age + offset(log(hours))
#>            Df Deviance    AIC     LRT Pr(>Chi)
#> <none>          74.458 274.19                 
#> sex         1   74.466 272.20 0.00802   0.9287
#> mother_age  2   75.599 271.33 1.14087   0.5653

# standard errors side by side
round(cbind(Poisson = sqrt(diag(vcov(pois_b))), NegBin = sqrt(diag(vcov(nb_b)))), 3)

#>               Poisson NegBin
#> (Intercept)     0.097  0.212
#> sexM            0.117  0.262
#> mother_ageYAF   0.151  0.338
#> mother_ageOAF   0.232  0.394


The estimates are similar, but the standard errors are roughly twice as large, and the apparent effect of the mother’s age class is no longer supported. The Poisson result relied on standard errors that were too small.





Exercise 6: predictions on the response scale
Compute the predicted number of approaches per hour, with 95% confidence intervals, for each mother’s age class (for female infants), from the negative binomial model.






Solution






nd <- data.frame(sex = factor("F", levels = levels(infants$sex)),
                 mother_age = factor(levels(infants$mother_age), levels = levels(infants$mother_age)),
                 hours = 1)                                    # rate per hour
pr <- predict(nb_b, newdata = nd, type = "link", se.fit = TRUE)
nd$rate <- exp(pr$fit)
nd$lo   <- exp(pr$fit - 1.96 * pr$se.fit)
nd$hi   <- exp(pr$fit + 1.96 * pr$se.fit)
nd

#>   sex mother_age hours      rate        lo       hi
#> 1   F        MAF     1 1.0301114 0.6798555 1.560816
#> 2   F        YAF     1 0.9898141 0.5480971 1.787515
#> 3   F        OAF     1 0.6853248 0.3375195 1.391535

ggplot(nd, aes(mother_age, rate)) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), colour = col_glm, size = .6) +
  labs(x = "Mother's age class", y = "Approaches per hour (female infants)")








Alternatively: emmeans::emmeans(nb_b, ~ mother_age, type = "response", offset = 0).





Exercise 7: report and reflect
Write two or three sentences reporting the results. Then check how many mothers contribute more than one infant to the data. Why could this be a problem, and what would you do about it?






Solution






sum(table(infants$mother) > 1)

#> [1] 16


Infants of the same mother are probably more similar to each other than infants of different mothers, so the observations are not fully independent. This can itself cause overdispersion and too small standard errors. The solution is a random intercept for mother: a GLMM, the topic of session 11.

set.seed(6)
group <- factor(rep(c("young", "old"), each = 25), levels = c("young", "old"))
y     <- rnorm(50, ifelse(group == "old", 12, 10), 3)

t.test(y ~ group, var.equal = TRUE)$statistic   # classic t-test

summary(lm(y ~ group))$coefficients             # same t (sign flipped), same p

Guiding principles

Model before data. Models follow from the research question, not from the data. Students simulate data from their model to understand it and to check design and power.

Real and simulated data. Real data from DPZ/CBB research show what analyses look like in practice; simulated data isolate exactly the aspect a session is about. Later, students work with their own projects.

title: Glossary
text:
Short explanations of terms that come up again and again. Labels show where a term is introduced: LM = Linear Models in R (with session number), ORES = Open, Replicable, and Ethical Science, TAE = Testing for Absence and Equivalence, IBCM = Inference with Bayesian Causal Models, WS = short workshops.
Entries marked Problem describe something that can go wrong, with steps towards a solution under What to do about it?

title: Glossary
text:
A

AIC (Akaike information criterion)
LM 09
A measure of how well a model predicts new data, balancing fit against the number of parameters. Lower is better. Only differences between models fitted to the same data are meaningful; ΔAIC < 2 means the models are hard to tell apart. See also model selection.


Alpha spending
ORES
In a sequential analysis, the overall type I error rate (α, usually .05) is distributed (“spent”) across the planned interim looks, so that the error rate over all looks stays at α. Common spending functions are Pocock and O’Brien–Fleming.


Assumptions (of the linear model)
LM 02–03
The linear model assumes that (1) observations are independent, (2) the relationship between predictors and response is linear (on the link scale), (3) residuals have constant variance (homoscedasticity) and (4) residuals are normally distributed. Independence matters most, normality least. Check assumptions with residual plots, not with significance tests.

title: Glossary
text:
B

Bayes factor
TAE
The ratio of how well two hypotheses predicted the observed data, e.g. BF01 = 5: the data are five times more likely under H0 than under H1. Unlike a p-value, it can quantify evidence for the null. Depends on the prior for the effect under H1, so report and justify it.


Bayesian model averaging
IBCM
Combining the predictions or estimates of several models, weighted by their posterior probabilities, instead of selecting a single model. Keeps uncertainty about which model is correct, e.g. about whether a causal link exists at all.

title: Glossary
text:
C

Causal Bayes net
IBCM
A directed graph whose arrows represent causal relations between variables, together with parameters that specify how causes produce their effects (e.g. causal strengths). Alternative graphs are alternative causal hypotheses that can be compared with data.


Causal strength
IBCM
How strongly a cause produces its effect, e.g. wc in a noisy-OR model: the probability that C produces E when no other cause does. Can be estimated with a posterior distribution and a credible interval. Cheng’s (1997) causal power is a classic point estimate.


Causal support
IBCM
Griffiths and Tenenbaum’s (2005) measure of the evidence for a causal link: the log ratio of the marginal likelihoods of the data under a structure with the link (S1) and without it (S0), log P(D | S1) / P(D | S0). Positive values favour a link.


Centring
LM 03, 05
Subtracting a value (usually the mean, or a meaningful reference such as trial 1) from a predictor. It changes the meaning of the intercept and of main effects in models with interactions, but not the fit of the model. See also z-transformation.


Collinearity
LM 03 Problem
Two or more predictors are strongly correlated, so the model cannot separate their effects. Symptoms: large standard errors, estimates that change a lot when a predictor is added or removed. Diagnose with variance inflation factors (car::vif(), performance::check_collinearity()); VIF > 5–10 is often taken as a warning sign.

What to do about it?

Ask whether both predictors are needed for the research question.
Combine them (e.g. into an index or a principal component) if they measure the same thing.
Accept wide intervals: collinearity is a property of the data, not an error. Do not drop predictors just to make p-values smaller.




Complete separation
LM 10 Problem
In a binomial model, a predictor (or combination) perfectly predicts the 0/1 outcome, e.g. all animals in one condition chose “yes”. The maximum-likelihood estimate is then infinite: huge estimates and standard errors, warnings such as “fitted probabilities numerically 0 or 1 occurred”.

What to do about it?

Check the cross-tabulation of predictor and response to find the cause.
Use penalised (Firth) logistic regression (logistf, brglm2) or a Bayesian model with a weakly informative prior.
Report the pattern descriptively; it may be the most informative result.




Confidence interval
LM 02
A range computed so that, across many repetitions of the study, 95% of such intervals contain the true value. It does not mean that this particular interval contains the true value with 95% probability; that is the interpretation of a Bayesian credible interval.


Contrasts and dummy coding
LM 04
How a categorical predictor is turned into numbers. Dummy (treatment) coding, R’s default, compares each level with a reference level. Sum coding compares each level with the grand mean, which makes main effects interpretable in models with interactions. Set with contrasts(); check what R did with model.matrix().


Convergence failure
LM 11 Problem
The fitting algorithm did not reliably find the maximum of the likelihood, e.g. lme4’s “Model failed to converge with max|grad| = …”. Common in mixed models with complex random effects, few levels of a grouping factor, or predictors on very different scales. The estimates may or may not be trustworthy.

What to do about it?

z-transform or rescale continuous predictors.
Try another optimizer: control = glmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa"), or compare all with allFit(). If they give the same estimates, the warning is usually a false alarm.
Increase the number of iterations, e.g. optCtrl = list(maxfun = 1e5).
Check for a singular fit; simplify the random-effects structure step by step (e.g. drop the correlations first: (1 + x || id)).
Consider glmmTMB or a Bayesian model (brms), where priors stabilise the fit.




Cook’s distance
LM 02
A measure of how much the model’s estimates change when a single observation is removed. Large values flag influential cases. See influential cases.


Credible interval
WS Bayes, TAE
In Bayesian statistics, an interval that contains the parameter with a given probability (e.g. 95%), given the model, the data and the prior.

title: Glossary
text:
D

Degrees of freedom
LM 02
Roughly, the number of observations minus the number of estimated parameters. They determine the shape of the t- and F-distributions used for tests. In mixed models they are not well defined, which is why lme4 reports no p-values for lmer().


Divergent transitions
WS Bayes Problem
A warning from Stan that the sampler had trouble exploring parts of the posterior. Even a few divergences can bias results.

What to do about it?

Increase adapt_delta (e.g. control = list(adapt_delta = 0.95)).
Use more informative priors, especially on standard deviations.
Simplify or reparameterise the model; check for weakly identified parameters.




Dummy coding
See contrasts and dummy coding.

title: Glossary
text:
E

Effect size
LM 02
How large an effect is, in units that matter: a raw difference (e.g. grams, seconds), a standardised difference (Cohen’s d), an odds ratio, or a change in probability. Report it with a confidence interval; a p-value alone says nothing about size.


Equivalence test (TOST)
TAE
Tests whether an effect is smaller than the smallest effect size of interest. Two one-sided tests check whether the effect is significantly above −SESOI and significantly below +SESOI. If both are significant, the effect is “statistically equivalent” to zero.


Estimated marginal means
LM 04
Model-based means for each level of a factor (or combination of factors), averaged over the other predictors. Computed with emmeans; the basis for pairwise comparisons and for reporting results on the response scale.

title: Glossary
text:
F

Failure to converge
See convergence failure.


Fixed effect
LM 11
A model parameter that is the same for all units, e.g. the average effect of age. In mixed models, contrasted with random effects, which vary between units.


Full–null model comparison
LM 09
Comparing the full model (with the predictors of interest) with a null model that lacks them but keeps all control predictors and random effects. A likelihood-ratio test of the two protects against cryptic multiple testing when there are several test predictors.

title: Glossary
text:
H

Heteroscedasticity
LM 02–03 Problem
The residual variance is not constant, e.g. it increases with the fitted values (a “funnel” in the residual plot). Standard errors and p-values can then be wrong.

What to do about it?

Ask whether the response type calls for a GLM (counts and proportions are heteroscedastic by nature).
Transform the response (e.g. log) if this is meaningful.
Model the variance explicitly (glmmTMB with dispformula, nlme::gls), or use robust standard errors (sandwich).

title: Glossary
text:
I

Influential cases
LM 02 Problem
Single observations that strongly change the results (see Cook’s distance), often outliers with unusual predictor values.

What to do about it?

Check for data errors first.
Fit the model with and without these cases and report both if conclusions differ.
Do not delete cases just because they are inconvenient; decide on exclusion rules in advance (see preregistration).




Interaction
LM 05
The effect of one predictor depends on the value of another, e.g. age affects foraging differently in two populations. In R: y ~ a * b. With an interaction in the model, the “main effects” are conditional effects at the zero point of the other predictor, so centring matters.


Intercept
LM 02
The predicted response when all predictors are zero (or at their reference level). Only meaningful if zero is a meaningful value, which is one reason for centring.

title: Glossary
text:
L

Likelihood-ratio test
LM 09–11
Compares two nested models by how much the likelihood improves with the extra parameters. In R: anova(m0, m1, test = "Chisq"). The standard way to test effects in GLMs and GLMMs.


Link function
LM 10
In a GLM, the function that connects the linear predictor to the expected response, e.g. the log link for counts (Poisson) and the logit link for probabilities (binomial). Coefficients are on the link scale; transform them back (e.g. exp(), plogis()) or plot predictions to interpret them.


Log-odds (logit)
LM 10
The scale of binomial models: log(p / (1 − p)). 0 corresponds to p = .5; ±2 to about .12 and .88. A coefficient is the change in log-odds per unit of the predictor; exp() turns it into an odds ratio.

title: Glossary
text:
M

Model selection
LM 09
Choosing among candidate models. For confirmatory questions, specify the model in advance and test it (e.g. full–null comparison). For exploratory or predictive questions, compare a small set of plausible models with AIC. Avoid stepwise selection by p-values (see overfitting).

title: Glossary
text:
O

Offset
LM 10
A term in a count model whose coefficient is fixed at 1, used when observation time or effort differs between observations. With a log link, offset(log(hours)) turns a model of counts into a model of rates (counts per hour), without estimating an extra parameter.


Noisy-OR
IBCM
A common assumption about how independent generative causes combine: each cause produces the effect independently with its own strength, so P(e | c, a) = wc + wa − wcwa when both are present.


Optional stopping
ORES Problem
Testing repeatedly as data come in and stopping as soon as p < .05. This inflates the type I error rate far above 5% (see the simulation on the ORES page).

What to do about it?

Fix the sample size in advance, based on a power analysis.
If you want to look early, plan a sequential analysis with alpha spending.
Bayesian analyses are less affected, but their error rates still depend on the stopping rule; plan it.




Overdispersion
LM 10 Problem
The data vary more than the model assumes. A Poisson model assumes variance = mean; real counts usually vary more. Ignoring it gives too small standard errors and too many false positives. Check with the ratio of residual deviance (or Pearson χ²) to residual df (≫ 1 is a warning sign), performance::check_overdispersion() or DHARMa.

What to do about it?

Check for missing predictors or non-independence first; overdispersion is often a symptom.
Use a negative binomial model (MASS::glm.nb, glmmTMB(family = nbinom2)).
In GLMMs, an observation-level random effect, (1 | obs), can absorb extra variation.
For many zeros, consider zero-inflation.




Overfitting
LM 09 Problem
The model fits noise in the sample rather than the underlying pattern, usually because it has too many parameters for the amount of data. It fits the sample well but predicts new data poorly, and its effects are overestimated.

What to do about it?

Limit the number of predictors (a common rule of thumb: at least 10–20 observations per parameter).
Specify the model from the research question, not from the data.
Evaluate predictions on new data or with cross-validation.

title: Glossary
text:
P

Partial pooling
LM 11
What random effects do: estimates for each individual are pulled towards the overall mean, more strongly for individuals with little data. A compromise between ignoring individuals (complete pooling) and estimating each one separately (no pooling).


Polynomial term
LM 08
A squared (or higher-order) predictor, e.g. y ~ age + I(age^2), to model curved relationships within the linear model. Centre the predictor first to reduce collinearity between the terms, or use poly().


Power
LM 08, WS Power
The probability of detecting an effect of a given size, if it exists. Depends on effect size, sample size, variability and α. For complex models, estimate it by simulation (see power analysis by simulation).


Preregistration
ORES
A time-stamped plan of hypotheses, design, sample size and analysis, written before the data are collected or seen. It separates confirmatory from exploratory analyses. Platforms: OSF, AsPredicted.


Prior, posterior
WS Bayes, TAE
In Bayesian statistics, the prior expresses what is plausible about a parameter before seeing the data; the posterior combines prior and data (via the likelihood). Check what your priors imply with a prior predictive check.


Pseudoreplication
LM 11 Problem
Treating repeated observations of the same unit (animal, group, session) as independent. The effective sample size is overstated, so standard errors are too small and false positives too frequent.

What to do about it?

Identify the unit of observation and all grouping factors before the analysis.
Include random effects for them, with random slopes for predictors that vary within units.
Alternatively, aggregate to one value per unit (loses information but is valid).




p-value
LM 02
The probability of a result at least as extreme as the observed one, if the null hypothesis were true. It is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true, and p > .05 is not evidence for “no effect” (see equivalence test).

title: Glossary
text:
R

Random effects (random intercepts and slopes)
LM 11
Parameters that vary between units of a grouping factor (e.g. chimps), modelled as coming from a common distribution. A random intercept, (1 | id), lets units differ in their baseline; a random slope, (1 + x | id), lets the effect of x differ between units. Random slopes are needed for predictors that vary within units, otherwise tests of these predictors are too liberal.


Reference level
LM 04
With dummy coding, the factor level that the intercept refers to and that all other levels are compared with. R uses the first level alphabetically; change it with relevel() or factor(..., levels = ).


Registered report
ORES
A publication format in which the introduction, methods and analysis plan are peer-reviewed before data collection. If accepted in principle, the paper is published regardless of the results.


Residuals
LM 02
Observed minus predicted values. Plots of residuals against fitted values and predictors are the main tool for checking assumptions. For GLMs and GLMMs, use simulated (quantile) residuals from DHARMa.


Rhat and effective sample size (ESS)
WS Bayes
Convergence diagnostics in Bayesian models. Rhat compares chains; values above 1.01 suggest they have not converged. ESS is the number of effectively independent draws; it should be at least a few hundred per parameter.


ROPE (region of practical equivalence)
TAE
A range of parameter values considered practically equivalent to zero (defined via the SESOI). If (almost) the whole posterior lies inside the ROPE, the effect is accepted as practically zero.


3Rs
ORES
Principles for the ethical use of animals in research: Replacement, Reduction and Refinement. Good statistical planning (power analysis, sequential designs) contributes directly to Reduction.

title: Glossary
text:
S

Sequential analysis
ORES
A design with planned interim analyses, at which data collection can stop for efficacy or futility, while alpha spending keeps the overall error rate at α. With animals, it reduces the expected number of animals needed. In R: rpact.


SESOI (smallest effect size of interest)
TAE
The smallest effect that would be theoretically or practically meaningful. Needed for equivalence tests, ROPEs and power analyses. Justify it from theory, previous studies or practical considerations, and preregister it.


Structure Induction (SI) model
IBCM
A Bayesian model of causal structure learning (Meder et al., 2014): it computes the posterior probability that a causal link exists, P(S1 | D), from a structure prior and the marginal likelihoods of the data under alternative causal structures. Makes the same assumptions as the causal support model.


Singular fit
LM 11 Problem
lme4’s message “boundary (singular) fit”: a random-effect variance is estimated as (nearly) zero or a correlation as ±1. The random-effects structure is too complex for the data, often because a grouping factor has few levels.

What to do about it?

Inspect VarCorr(model) to see which component is at the boundary.
Simplify: first remove the random-effect correlations (||), then random slopes with (near-)zero variance, guided by the design rather than by p-values.
Keep in mind that removing random slopes for within-unit predictors makes tests of these predictors too liberal; report what you did.
A Bayesian model (brms) with weakly informative priors avoids estimates at the boundary.




Standard error
LM 02
The standard deviation of an estimate across repeated samples: how much the estimate would vary if the study were repeated. The basis of confidence intervals and tests.


Stopping for futility
ORES
Ending a study early at a planned interim analysis because the effect is unlikely to reach significance even with the full sample. Saves resources and, in animal research, animals.

title: Glossary
text:
Z

z-transformation (standardisation)
LM 03
Subtracting the mean of a predictor and dividing by its standard deviation: scale(x). The predictor then has mean 0 and SD 1, so coefficients are the effect of a one-SD change. Makes effects of predictors on different scales comparable and often helps models to converge.


Zero-inflation
LM 10, WS GLMMs Problem
More zeros than a Poisson or negative binomial model predicts, e.g. because some animals never show a behaviour. Ignoring it can bias estimates. Check with DHARMa::testZeroInflation() or performance::check_zeroinflation().

What to do about it?

Ask where the extra zeros come from (e.g. animals that were never in a position to show the behaviour).
Fit a zero-inflated or hurdle model with glmmTMB (ziformula = ~ 1); see advanced GLMMs.
Sometimes a negative binomial model alone already accounts for the zeros; compare the models.

title: Inference with Bayesian Causal Models
text: A hands-on course that brings together statistical inference and causal inference. Most statistical models answer “how strongly are X and Y related?”. Causal models ask “does X cause Y, and how strongly?”. Bayesian causal models answer both questions in one framework: we specify alternative causal structures as hypotheses, and update our beliefs about them, and about the strength of causal links, in light of data.

title: Inference with Bayesian Causal Models
text:
Topics

Causal Bayes nets: representing causal hypotheses as graphs with parameters
Causal structure induction: Bayesian updating over alternative causal structures; the causal support model (Griffiths & Tenenbaum, 2005) and the Structure Induction (SI) model (Meder et al., 2014)
Causal strength: Bayesian estimation of the strength of a causal link, with credible intervals
Priors: structure priors and parameter priors, and how they shape conclusions from limited data (Stephan & Waldmann, 2026)
Bayesian model averaging: combining uncertainty about structure and strength
From 2×2 tables to richer structures: multiple causes, common causes and causal chains

Outcome: each participant formulates competing causal hypotheses for their own research question and evaluates them with a Bayesian causal model.
Prerequisites: Linear Models in R. The short workshop Bayesian modelling with brms is a helpful complement.

Key terms: Causal Bayes net, Noisy-OR, Causal support, Structure Induction (SI) model, Causal strength, Bayesian model averaging, Prior, posterior

title: Inference with Bayesian Causal Models
section: Worked example: does C cause E?
text:
Worked example: does C cause E?
The simplest causal inference problem: we observe whether a potential cause C is present or absent, and whether an effect E occurs. The data form a 2×2 contingency table. Two causal structures could have generated them:










Under S1, E is produced by C (with causal strength wc) and by unobserved background causes A (strength wa). The two causes combine as a noisy-OR: P(e+ | c+) = wc + wa − wcwa, and P(e+ | c−) = wa.
Under S0, there is no link: E is produced by A only, so P(e+ | c+) = P(e+ | c−) = wa.
A third parameter, the base rate bc of C, is part of both structures. With the same prior in both, it cancels from the comparison, so we leave it out below.


The data

# Table 1: positive contingency
d1 <- c(n_ce = 16, n_c = 20,    # E present in 16 of 20 cases with C
        n_nce = 8, n_nc = 20)   # E present in  8 of 20 cases without C

# Table 2: zero contingency, high outcome density (a classic "causal illusion" set)
d2 <- c(n_ce = 10, n_c = 10,
        n_nce = 10, n_nc = 10)

Step 1: how likely are the data under each structure?
Bayesian inference compares structures by their marginal likelihood: how probable the data are under a structure, averaged over all values of its parameters, weighted by the parameter priors. As in the standard SI model, we use flat Beta(1, 1) priors for wc and wa. With two parameters, a fine grid is enough to compute the integral.

si_model <- function(n_ce, n_c, n_nce, n_nc, prior_s1 = .5,
                     wc_prior = c(1, 1), wa_prior = c(1, 1), grid = 401) {
  w <- (seq_len(grid) - .5) / grid            # grid over (0, 1)

  # S1: noisy-OR of C (wc, rows) and A (wa, columns)
  p_c   <- outer(w, w, function(wc, wa) wc + wa - wc * wa)  # P(e+|c+)
  p_nc  <- matrix(w, grid, grid, byrow = TRUE)               # P(e+|c-)
  lik1  <- exp(n_ce * log(p_c)  + (n_c  - n_ce)  * log1p(-p_c) +
               n_nce * log(p_nc) + (n_nc - n_nce) * log1p(-p_nc))
  prior <- outer(dbeta(w, wc_prior[1], wc_prior[2]),
                 dbeta(w, wa_prior[1], wa_prior[2])) / grid^2
  ml1   <- sum(lik1 * prior)                   # marginal likelihood P(D | S1)

  # S0: only A, so P(e+ | c+) = P(e+ | c-) = wa
  lik0 <- w^(n_ce + n_nce) * (1 - w)^(n_c - n_ce + n_nc - n_nce)
  ml0  <- sum(lik0 * dbeta(w, wa_prior[1], wa_prior[2]) / grid)  # P(D | S0)

  post_w <- lik1 * prior / sum(lik1 * prior)   # joint posterior of wc, wa (S1)
  list(ml1 = ml1, ml0 = ml0,
       # causal support (Griffiths & Tenenbaum, 2005)
       support = log(ml1 / ml0),
       # SI model: posterior probability of S1
       p_s1 = prior_s1 * ml1 / (prior_s1 * ml1 + (1 - prior_s1) * ml0),
       # marginal posterior of wc under S1
       w = w, wc_post = rowSums(post_w))
}

r1 <- do.call(si_model, as.list(d1))
r2 <- do.call(si_model, as.list(d2))



Step 2: posterior probability of a causal link
Bayes’ rule combines the marginal likelihoods with the structure prior P(S1):
\[
P(S_1 \mid D) = \frac{P(D \mid S_1)\,P(S_1)}{P(D \mid S_1)\,P(S_1) + P(D \mid S_0)\,P(S_0)}
\]










Table

P(S1 | D), prior 0.5




1: positive contingency (ΔP = 0.40)
2.81
0.94


2: zero contingency (ΔP = 0)
0.31
0.58






Table 1: the data clearly favour a causal link, P(S1 | D) = 0.94.
Table 2: although ΔP = 0, the posterior rises above the prior of 0.5. Ceiling data leave the strength of C undetermined: E may be fully produced by A, with C’s influence masked. S1 is consistent with the data over a wider range of parameters than S0, which needs wa ≈ 1. A non-zero belief in a link after zero-contingency data is therefore not necessarily a bias, but can be the result of rational Bayesian updating (Stephan & Waldmann, 2026).

How the posterior depends on the structure prior:


Code
priors <- seq(0, 1, by = .01)
pp <- rbind(
  data.frame(table = "Table 1: positive contingency", prior = priors,
             post = priors * r1$ml1 / (priors * r1$ml1 + (1 - priors) * r1$ml0)),
  data.frame(table = "Table 2: zero contingency",    prior = priors,
             post = priors * r2$ml1 / (priors * r2$ml1 + (1 - priors) * r2$ml0)))

ggplot(pp, aes(prior, post, colour = table)) +
  geom_abline(linetype = 2, colour = col_muted) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(col_s1, col_s0), name = NULL) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(x = "Prior P(S1)", y = "Posterior P(S1 | D)", caption = "Dashed: no change from prior to posterior") +
  theme(legend.position = "right")











Step 3: what if we are unsure about the prior?
So far the structure prior was a fixed number. Often we are not sure which prior is appropriate. We can express this uncertainty as a distribution over the prior, P(S1) ~ Beta(a, b), and propagate it: each possible prior gives a posterior P(S1 | D). The result is a distribution over the posterior probability of a link, which we can summarise with a 95% interval. We compare an uninformed learner, P(S1) ~ Beta(1, 1), with a sceptical one, P(S1) ~ Beta(2, 8), who expects links to be rare.

post_s1 <- function(prior, r) prior * r$ml1 / (prior * r$ml1 + (1 - prior) * r$ml0)

set.seed(1)
draws <- list(uninformed = rbeta(1e5, 1, 1),   # P(S1) ~ Beta(1, 1)
              sceptical  = rbeta(1e5, 2, 8))   # P(S1) ~ Beta(2, 8), mean 0.2

summ <- function(x) c(mean = mean(x), quantile(x, c(.025, .975)))
round(rbind(`Table 1, uninformed` = summ(post_s1(draws$uninformed, r1)),
            `Table 1, sceptical`  = summ(post_s1(draws$sceptical,  r1)),
            `Table 2, uninformed` = summ(post_s1(draws$uninformed, r2)),
            `Table 2, sceptical`  = summ(post_s1(draws$sceptical,  r2))), 2)

#>                     mean 2.5% 97.5%
#> Table 1, uninformed 0.87 0.29  1.00
#> Table 1, sceptical  0.74 0.32  0.94
#> Table 2, uninformed 0.55 0.03  0.98
#> Table 2, sceptical  0.25 0.04  0.56




Code
pu <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(draws), function(p) rbind(
  data.frame(prior = p, table = "Table 1: positive contingency", x = post_s1(draws[[p]], r1)),
  data.frame(prior = p, table = "Table 2: zero contingency",    x = post_s1(draws[[p]], r2)))))
pu$prior <- factor(pu$prior, levels = c("uninformed", "sceptical"),
                   labels = c("Uninformed: P(S1) ~ Beta(1, 1)", "Sceptical: P(S1) ~ Beta(2, 8)"))
ci <- aggregate(x ~ prior + table, pu, function(v) quantile(v, c(.025, .975)))
ci <- data.frame(ci[, 1:2], lo = ci$x[, 1], hi = ci$x[, 2])

ggplot(pu, aes(x, fill = table)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = 50, alpha = .6, position = "identity") +
  geom_errorbarh(data = ci, aes(y = -0.4, xmin = lo, xmax = hi, colour = table),
                 inherit.aes = FALSE, height = .3, linewidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~ prior, ncol = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(col_s1, col_s0), name = NULL) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(col_s1, col_s0), guide = "none") +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(-0.6, 8)) +
  labs(x = "Posterior P(S1 | D)", y = "Density", caption = "Bars: 95% intervals") +
  theme(legend.position = "top")









The interval shows how much the conclusion depends on prior assumptions. With Table 1, both learners end up favouring a link, but the sceptic is less sure. With Table 2, the conclusion is driven almost entirely by the prior: the data cannot settle whether C causes E.


Step 4: how strong is the causal link?
Structure induction asks whether C causes E. Causal strength asks how strongly. Within S1, the posterior distribution of wc follows directly from the grid computed in Step 1 (cf. Lu et al., 2008, for Bayesian strength learning). For comparison, the classic point estimate is Cheng’s (1997) causal power, ΔP / (1 − P(e+ | c−)).

wc_summary <- function(r) {
  cdf <- cumsum(r$wc_post)
  c(mean = sum(r$w * r$wc_post),
    lower = r$w[which(cdf >= .025)[1]], upper = r$w[which(cdf >= .975)[1]])
}
round(rbind(`Table 1` = wc_summary(r1), `Table 2` = wc_summary(r2)), 2)

#>         mean lower upper
#> Table 1 0.59  0.19  0.86
#> Table 2 0.55  0.03  0.98

(16/20 - 8/20) / (1 - 8/20)    # causal power for Table 1

#> [1] 0.6666667




Code
sp <- rbind(data.frame(table = "Table 1: positive contingency", w = r1$w, dens = r1$wc_post * length(r1$w)),
            data.frame(table = "Table 2: zero contingency",    w = r2$w, dens = r2$wc_post * length(r2$w)))
ggplot(sp, aes(w, dens, colour = table, fill = table)) +
  geom_area(alpha = .25, position = "identity") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = (16/20 - 8/20) / (1 - 8/20), linetype = 2, colour = col_s1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(col_s1, col_s0), name = NULL) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(col_s1, col_s0), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = expression(paste("Causal strength ", w[c])), y = "Posterior density (under S1)",
       caption = "Dashed: causal power for Table 1") +
  theme(legend.position = "top")










Table 1: the posterior peaks near the causal power, but the 95% credible interval is wide: 40 observations say that C causes E, but not precisely how strongly.
Table 2: the posterior is very broad. Ceiling data are compatible with almost any strength of C, because A already produces E every time.



Step 5: combining structure and strength
The strength estimate above assumes that the link exists. Bayesian model averaging keeps the uncertainty about structure: with probability P(S0 | D), wc is exactly 0; with probability P(S1 | D), it follows the posterior under S1.

bma <- function(r) {
  p_zero <- 1 - r$p_s1                                   # probability that wc = 0
  c(`P(wc = 0)` = p_zero, `mean wc` = r$p_s1 * wc_summary(r)[["mean"]])
}
round(rbind(`Table 1` = bma(r1), `Table 2` = bma(r2)), 2)

#>         P(wc = 0) mean wc
#> Table 1      0.06    0.56
#> Table 2      0.42    0.32


This is the step from statistical to causal inference: the question is not only how large an effect is, but which causal structure generated the data, and what follows for the strength of the link if we are uncertain about the structure.

section: Worked example: do chimpanzees understand mechanisms?
text:
Worked example: do chimpanzees understand mechanisms?
Chimpanzees choose into which of two boxes a grape is dropped. The Safe box clearly guarantees delivery; in the Risky box, the grape seems to get stuck. In fact, both boxes always deliver.


RQ1: Do chimps prefer the Safe box in session 1?

RQ2: Does this preference change over sessions? (Curiosity → below 50%? Indifference → towards 50%? Utility → stays Safe?)


Ongoing study with the MPI EVA, Leipzig; preregistered. The data do not exist yet: the numbers below are made up to reflect what we expect. A small example: 10 chimps × 4 sessions × 10 trials; response: choice (1 = Safe, 0 = Risky).

The data

# Safe choices (out of 10) of 10 chimps in sessions 1-4
K <- rbind(c( 9, 10, 10, 10), c(10,  9,  9,  8), c(10, 10,  9,  7), c(10, 10,  6,  8),
           c( 5,  8,  8,  8), c( 8,  6,  6,  3), c( 5,  3,  2,  4), c( 5,  2,  3,  3),
           c( 1,  0,  1,  0), c( 1,  0,  0,  0))
cd <- data.frame(chimp = factor(rep(1:10, 4)), session = rep(1:4, each = 10), safe = c(K))

# trial-level data (what the models are fitted to): one row per choice
set.seed(11)
trials <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(cd)), function(i)
  data.frame(chimp = cd$chimp[i], session = cd$session[i],
             trial = (cd$session[i] - 1) * 10 + 1:10,
             choice = sample(rep(c(1, 0), c(cd$safe[i], 10 - cd$safe[i]))))))
trials$session_c <- trials$session - 1          # session 1 = 0

ggplot(cd, aes(session, p, group = chimp, colour = chimp)) +
  geom_line(alpha = .6) + geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  scale_colour_viridis_d(end = .9, guide = "none") +
